Going out at night or being outside after dark
Any form of physical contact with others

When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

vignette: Jamal, a nineteen‑year‑old African American detective, had never imagined that a routine stakeout would become the source of a lifetime of dread. On a rainy Friday night in June, he was tracking a known suspect through a vacant warehouse on the outskirts of town when a sudden ambush sent him into the basement of a derelict storage unit. The suspect’s crew had cornered him, silenced his radio, and chained him to a concrete slab for two harrowing weeks. The only light came from a flickering fluorescent tube, the air hung with the stale smell of rust, and the constant low groan of metal as a passing truck rattled the walls. He watched as other victims, strangers to his world, were forced to endure the same cramped darkness, their faces blurred in his mind. When he was finally released, the physical wounds had faded, but the memory of those damp walls and the guttural sound of the chains was indelibly etched into his mind. The memory has, for Jamal, become a living, breathing entity. He can’t find the words that would adequately describe the terror; the experience sits at the back of his mind like a locked box. When he attempts to articulate it, the vocabulary he needs seems to slip away, leaving him in a state of helpless silence. Even more unsettling, the sounds from that basement— the metallic clank of a chain, the distant echo of a frightened voice—recur in his mind at random moments, sometimes in the middle of a meeting or during a quiet night in his apartment. When these auditory echoes surface, a wave of raw emotion washes over him, but it is not accompanied by any clear visual image; it is a feeling of being utterly trapped, of the world collapsing, without a picture to anchor it. That disorienting combination of feeling and lack of words has driven Jamal to adopt a series of maladaptive strategies: he tries hard not to think about the incident, he shuns any nighttime outings, and he refuses physical contact from anyone, even his girlfriend, who has begged him to touch his hand after a long day. Because the memory’s haunting qualities are so powerful, the strategies become an automatic response. Every time the echo of the chain’s rattling or the memory of the dim basement lights intrudes on his thoughts, Jamal’s first instinct is to suppress the thought entirely, pushing it to the back of his mind. He has learned to avoid any situation that could trigger that memory, especially when it is dark outside. Nighttime is the single most frightening period for him; the streetlights flicker, and every shadow feels like a potential threat. Consequently, he no longer participates in the night stakeouts that are a core part of his detective work. This avoidance of darkness has caused him to miss critical pieces of evidence, leading to several stalled investigations. At the same time, his refusal to be touched has frayed the relationship with his girlfriend, Mara. She is a bright, empathetic nurse who has often tried to console him with a hug, but Jamal, believing any contact might resurrect the phantom sounds from the basement, distances himself, which only deepens his sense of isolation. During the first months after his release, Jamal would sit for hours in the interrogation room, staring at the ceiling while the interrogation staff spoke of other cases. He’d listen to their voices, but his mind would drift to the dim basement, to the sounds that haunted him. When the memory rose, the suppression would fail, and he would burst into tears, his throat tight with the impossible feeling of being trapped again. The experience left him exhausted, and he began to dread every interrogation, every night shift, and every hug from Mara. As weeks turned into months, his avoidance behaviors became more rigid. He started to see his job as a source of danger rather than a duty, and the once-bright curiosity that had drawn him to law enforcement turned into a fearful dread of the unknown. The cumulative effect of these avoidance strategies has now brought Jamal to the threshold of therapy. He can no longer afford to miss stakeouts— a decision that has left his supervisor questioning his reliability. Moreover, the strain with Mara threatens to dissolve the only stable relationship he has. Jamal’s most profound fear is that the suppression he has relied on will ultimately crush the remaining aspects of his life; he hopes that through therapy he can find a way to confront the memory, speak the words that have eluded him, and reclaim the nights, the touch, and his role as a detective.
